newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan courtmartial to try killer of Israeli girls.
newsitem.headline: Jordan courtmartial to try killer of Israeli girls.

text.p: A Jordanian soldier who shot dead seven Israeli schoolgirls at a Jordan Valley border post goes on trial for his life in a military court on Tuesday charged with premeditated murder.
Army driver Ahmed al-Daqamsa, 26, emptied three rifle clips at the teenage girls as they visited the lush farmlands of Baqoura, known in Israel as the Island of Peace, on March 13.
Daqamsa, who faces the gallows if found guilty, confessed to the shooting but said he had reacted impulsively when the girls teased him while he prayed, his lawyer Ahmed Nijdawi said.
"He admitted that he opened fire. But it was not planned," Nijdawi told Reuters.

The shooting, on Jordanian border land leased to Israel under a 1994 peace accord, rattled an already tense Middle East and highlighted deep unease in Jordan over the treaty. It also revived charges in Jordan that by leasing the land to Israel, Jordan had surrendered territory to its former enemy.
King Hussein flew to Jerusalem to console Israeli relatives of the girls, aged 13 and 14, and said Daqamsa should have been shot dead on the spot by his army comrades.

But while government officials condemned the killing as a vile and criminal act, Jordan's vocal peace critics have said Daqamsa's motives were patriotic. They blamed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for provoking Arabs by approving Jewish settlements around Arab East Jerusalem.
"People feel he is not guilty, that he is a national hero," Nijdawi said.
Daqamsa will face a panel of five military judges when the trial opens at an army base near Naour, a few miles (km) south of Amman, on Tuesday.

Nijdawi said the court would read out the charges of premeditated killing, attempt to kill and military sedition. Daqamsa would enter a plea and the trial would probably adjourn for a few days before witnesses were called.
"He will tell the court he is not guilty," Nijdawi said.

He said the charge sheet stated that Daqamsa had planned to kill Israelis in the past but held back. On the day of the shooting he left alone the first group of Israelis who visited Baqoura because they were under 10 years old, it said.
When the next batch of slightly older students came he fired off three ammunition clips from a distance of 30 metres (yards) before his rifle jammed, it said.
Nijdawi said other Jordanian lawyers planned to participate in Daqamsa's defence. Moroccan and Tunisian lawyers had also volunteered their support.

In March police had to set up roadblocks to prevent sympathisers from converging on Daqamsa's village in northern Jordan in a gesture of solidarity with his family, who said they suffered years ago from repeated Israeli military bombardments.
Last week the head of Jordan's influential Islamist-leaning engineers' union unveiled a large car sticker on his windscreen announcing: "We love Daqamsa. We love the Arab army."
